messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 55
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Farmer
  trauma_type: Assault
  pcl5: 76

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Somatic (Heart Racing): Own heart racing or pounding, Olfactory (Sweat/Body): Sweat or body odour, Perceived Threat: People acting suspiciously
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rumination: Revenge: ruminate about how to get even with assailant, Avoid Anniversaries: Dates or anniversaries connected to the event, Overworking: I throw myself into work or tasks to keep my mind occupied
  Memory: Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me, Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Ali, a 55-year-old farmer, had been married for thirty years and raised three children on the land his father had worked before him. The assault happened two years ago, on the morning of the harvest festival. He had gone into town to buy seed, and in the alley behind the supply store a man he did not know grabbed him from behind, slammed his head against the brick wall, and took his wallet and his wedding ring. Ali did not fight back. He remembered the pressure of the stranger’s forearm against his throat, the sour smell of sweat and old clothing filling his nose, and then nothing but jagged pieces—a broken fingernail scraping his cheek, the weight of his own heart thudding so violently it seemed to shake his ribs, the glint of the shop window reflected in a puddle. The memory never came as a single story. It arrived in fragments that did not fit together, as if they belonged to someone else’s life. When his wife asked him what happened at the hospital, he tried to describe the alley, the grip, the smell, but the words slipped away and he ended up staring at the floor, unable to finish.

In the months that followed, Ali found himself working longer and longer hours in the fields. He was up before dawn, out past dusk, weeding, watering, repairing fences—anything that kept his hands busy and his mind fixed on the next task. He told himself it was the season, that the crops needed him. But what he did not say was that when he stopped, the fragments came back, and with them a tightness in his chest and a hot, circling anger. He would catch himself imagining ways to get even with the man who had taken his ring, planning confrontations that would never happen, replaying blow after blow in his head until his jaw ached. The anniversary of the assault arrived, and though he told no one, he made sure he was far from town that day—he drove out to the far pasture and did not come home until after dark. He could not explain why the date mattered so much; the memory itself was still a blur, but the feeling of that morning returned like a physical weight.

His wife noticed the changes. He had stopped going to the weekly market, claiming it was too far or too hot. He avoided the corner of the supply store where the alley opened onto the street. When she asked about the trip to town, he said he sent their son instead. She did not press. At home, he was quiet, easily startled if she came up behind him. The smell of his own sweat after a long day in the sun began to make his stomach turn—he started showering twice, then three times a day, scrubbing his skin until it was raw. The rapid thump of his heart during exertion, something he had never noticed before, now made him pause in the field, listening to it pound, certain it meant something was about to go wrong again. He watched people warily. A stranger lingering too long at the edge of his property, a neighbor who seemed to be watching him, a car that slowed near his gate—each one triggered a tightening in his chest and a flicker of the alley, of the sour smell, of the pressure on his throat.

He came to the clinic only because his wife insisted, her voice tight with worry. He sat on the edge of the chair, his hands clasped, his eyes on the floor. He said he did not know why he was there. He said he just wanted to be left alone to work his land. But when asked what he was afraid of, he could not answer—not because he did not want to, but because the fear itself was a fragment, a smell, a pounding in his ears, a nameless threat that hovered at the edge of every quiet moment. He hoped, without quite believing it, that maybe someone could help him fit the pieces together so they stopped feeling like they belonged to a stranger. He feared most that the man who attacked him was still out there, and that one day, for no reason he could understand, Ali would find himself back in that alley again.
